n: Judah’s land is described first and in the most detail, fitting its role as the tribe of future kings. Its southern edge touched Edom and the dry wilderness of Zin.

f.g: Land was assigned by casting lots, which Israel saw as letting the Lord decide (Proverbs 16:33).

n: The southern border starts at the southern tip of the Dead Sea, called here “the salt sea” because its water is so salty nothing lives in it.

f.g: The Dead Sea, the lowest body of water on earth.

n: The line runs southwest past the Scorpion Pass and Kadesh-barnea, the oasis where Israel camped for many years during the wilderness wandering.

f.g: Means “ascent of scorpions,” a steep pass south of the Dead Sea.
Made a turn; curved around.

n: The border reaches the “river of Egypt,” a seasonal stream bed, and ends at the Mediterranean. This matches the southern border the Lord had given Moses.

f.g: Usually identified with Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai, not the Nile.

f.w: this shall be your south coast

n: The Dead Sea forms Judah’s east side. The northern border begins where the Jordan River flows into the Dead Sea.

f.g: The mouth of the Jordan, where it empties into the Dead Sea.

n: The northern line climbs west from the Jordan valley. The “stone of Bohan” was a known landmark, apparently named after a Reubenite.

f.g: A site near the Jordan, just north of the Dead Sea.

n: The border passes the valley of Achor, where Achan was judged, and climbs toward the springs below Jerusalem. En-rogel was a spring just south of the city.
The line skirts the south side of Jerusalem along the valley of Hinnom, placing the city itself just inside Benjamin’s land. The Jebusites still held it.

f.w: valley of the son of Hinnom
f.g: Later infamous for child sacrifice; its Hebrew name (Ge-hinnom) became “Gehenna,” a symbol of hell.

n: From the hills west of Jerusalem the border runs to Kirjath-jearim, the town where the ark of the covenant would later rest for many years.

f.g: Often identified with the spring at Lifta, just northwest of Jerusalem.

n: The line descends westward out of the hills to Beth-shemesh and Timnah, the lowland towns that later figure in the stories of the ark and of Samson.
The border passes north of Ekron, a Philistine city, and reaches the Mediterranean at Jabneel. Much of this coastland stayed in Philistine hands for centuries.
The Mediterranean (“the great sea”) is the western boundary. The full outline of Judah’s inheritance is now complete.

f.g: The Mediterranean Sea.

n: Caleb receives Hebron, just as Moses had promised him for following the Lord wholeheartedly. Faithfulness forty-five years earlier is now rewarded.

f.g: Where Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were buried.

n: Caleb, now in his eighties, drives out the very giants whose size had frightened Israel’s spies decades before. Faith overcomes the old fear.

f.g: The Anakim were remembered as a tall, fearsome people.

n: Caleb moves on to Debir. Its older name, Kirjath-sepher, means “city of the book,” possibly hinting at a center of writing or records.

f.g: Hebrew “town of the book/scribe.”

n: Caleb offers his daughter in marriage to whoever captures the city — a custom that rewarded courage and tied a brave man into the family.
Othniel, Caleb’s younger relative, takes the city and marries Achsah. He later becomes the first judge of Israel.
Achsah urges her husband to ask for a field, then comes to her father herself. Her getting down from the donkey was a gesture of respect before making a request.

f.g: Got down from her donkey.
“What do you want?”

n: Achsah boldly asks for springs, since dry southern land is useless without water. Caleb generously gives both upper and lower springs — a small picture of a father who loves to give.

f.g: Hebrew Negev, the dry south.
Nether = lower.

n: A summary line introducing the town lists that follow. These lists worked like a land deed for each family of Judah.
The first district is the Negev, the far south near Edom. Towns are grouped by region, like counties on a map.

f.g: Toward the border of Edom.

n: More southern towns. Most of these were small settlements in the dry country where flocks were grazed.

f.g: Possibly linked to the Kenites, who lived in this region.

n: Two places named Hazor appear in Judah’s south; this is not the great northern city Joshua burned.

f.g: “Hazor” means enclosure or settlement, a common place name.

n: Ziph appears again in the hill-country list; there may have been two towns with the same name.
Kerioth may be the hometown of Judas Iscariot, whose surname is often explained as “man of Kerioth,” though this is uncertain.

f.g: Some scholars connect “Iscariot” with Hebrew ish Kerioth, “man of Kerioth.”

n: Moladah and nearby towns were later shared with the tribe of Simeon, whose land lay inside Judah’s.
Several names begin with “Hazar,” meaning a settlement or encampment — fitting for herdsmen in the desert fringe.

f.g: Hazar = village or enclosure.

n: Beer-sheba, the well where Abraham and Isaac made covenants, marked Israel’s southern limit: “from Dan to Beer-sheba.”
Three more southern towns. This Baalah is a different place from the Baalah (Kirjath-jearim) on the northern border.

f.g: A name meaning “lady” or tied to Baal worship; several towns bore it.

n: Hormah, “destruction,” recalls where Israel was once defeated and later victorious in the wilderness years.
Ziklag later became David’s base when he hid from Saul among the Philistines.
The southern district closes with a total of twenty-nine cities and their surrounding villages, which were small unwalled farm settlements.

f.g: Unwalled hamlets that depended on a nearby walled town.

n: Now the Shephelah, the fertile foothills west of the mountains. Zoreah and Eshtaol are the home district of Samson.

f.g: Hebrew Shephelah, the low rolling hills between the mountains and the coast.

n: More foothill towns. The repetition of names across regions reminds us that these were real villages known to the first readers.

f.g: Means “spring of gardens.”

n: Adullam had caves where David later hid; Socoh and Azekah frame the valley where David fought Goliath.
The first group of foothill towns totals fourteen. (The list has fifteen names; scholars think one may be a second name or a copying variation.)

f.g: Totals in these lists sometimes differ slightly from the names given.

n: A second foothill district begins, further south and west toward Philistine territory.

f.g: Migdal = tower.

n: Mizpeh means “watchtower”; several towns in Israel carried this name.

f.g: Hebrew “lookout point.” Not the Benjamite Mizpeh of Judges 20.

n: Lachish and Eglon were major fortified cities Joshua had defeated in the southern campaign.
Three more small towns of the western foothills, probably farming villages now hard to locate.

f.g: Location uncertain.

n: This district closes with Makkedah, the cave-town where the five Amorite kings were caught.

f.g: “House of Dagon,” named for a Philistine god.

n: A third foothill district. Libnah was a Levite city and one Joshua had taken.
Another Ashnah — a second town by that name in the foothills.

f.g: Different from the Ashnah of verse 33.

n: Keilah was a town David later rescued from the Philistines. Mareshah was the hometown of the prophet Micah’s region.
Ekron, one of the five Philistine cities, is assigned to Judah. The allotment states God’s promise even where conquest was not yet complete.

f.g: Literally “daughters” — dependent towns of a mother city.

n: The coastal plain from Ekron to the sea, including the area around Ashdod, is listed as part of Judah’s inheritance.
Ashdod and Gaza were strong Philistine cities. Judah was given them on paper but held them only briefly; the gift waited on Israel’s faithfulness.
Now the hill country, Judah’s heartland. Jattir later received a share of David’s spoil.
Debir is mentioned again under another name, showing that towns often had more than one name over time.

f.g: Another name for Debir (see verse 15).

n: Anab was a town of the Anakim that Joshua had cleared.
Giloh was the hometown of Ahithophel, David’s counselor who later betrayed him. This Goshen is a town in Judah, not the region in Egypt.
Another cluster of hill-country towns around Hebron.

f.g: Means “silence.”

n: Beth-tappuah means “house of the apple (or apricot),” likely named for its orchards.

f.g: Tappuah = apple or similar fruit.

n: Hebron is listed under its old name, Kirjath-arba. It became David’s first capital.
Maon and Carmel are where Nabal and Abigail lived. This Carmel is a town south of Hebron, not Mount Carmel.
This Jezreel is a small town in Judah, home of David’s wife Ahinoam, not the northern valley.
Cain here is a town name (perhaps tied to the Kenites), and Gibeah means “hill”; neither is the well-known person or Saul’s town.

f.g: Hebrew “hill.” Saul’s Gibeah was in Benjamin.

n: Beth-zur, north of Hebron, became an important fortress guarding the road to Jerusalem.
A small group of six towns. The Greek Septuagint adds a further district here that includes Bethlehem, which the Hebrew text lacks.

f.g: The Septuagint inserts eleven more towns after this verse, including Bethlehem and Tekoa.

n: Kirjath-baal, another name for Kirjath-jearim, shows how names tied to Baal were sometimes replaced over time.
The final district is the wilderness of Judah, the dry land sloping to the Dead Sea where David later hid from Saul.

f.g: Possibly near Qumran, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found.

n: En-gedi, a lush spring in the desert cliffs above the Dead Sea, became a famous hiding place and garden spot.

f.g: Location uncertain; near the Dead Sea.

n: An honest note: Judah could not take Jerusalem. It stayed Jebusite until David captured it centuries later. The phrase “unto this day” shows the writer lived before David’s conquest.

f.g: Up to the time the book was written.
